117.subtitle: Soft arms on the great mountain, and an empire

commentary.meaning: Five names, and the verse works by placing things next to each other that do not obviously belong together. It begins by fixing her address — the great Kailāsa, the snow peak of the north where Śiva sits — and then, instead of describing a throne or a retinue, describes her arms, which are said to be as soft as the thread inside a lotus stalk and to curve like creepers. That is the vocabulary of court poetry, not of theology, and it arrives long after the head-to-foot description that occupies the opening of the hymn has been completed and left behind. From there the verse moves to what is owed her: she is mahanīyā, to be honoured, a gerundive that states an obligation rather than pays a compliment. Then compassion, not as something she feels but as the shape she has taken. And then, in the last and longest name, empire. The sequence runs from a mountain to a stalk of lotus fibre to universal sovereignty in the space of thirty-two syllables, and the softness sits in the middle of it, holding the two ends apart.
commentary.history:
Kailāsa is a real mountain, a peak of roughly six and a half thousand metres in what is now western Tibet, north of the Himālayan range proper and unclimbed by consent. It is circumambulated by Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and adherents of Bön. In Sanskrit literature it is the seat of Śiva and Pārvatī, the place from which the epics and Purāṇas repeatedly begin a scene; Kubera's city of Alakā is set in its neighbourhood, which is why Kālidāsa's cloud is sent there; and it is the mountain Rāvaṇa is said to have tried to lift, until Śiva pressed it down with a toe and pinned him under it for an age.

The hymn says mahākailāsa, the great Kailāsa, and the qualifier is doing work. The commentators generally take it to mark off a Kailāsa that is not the geographical one, on the reasonable ground that the goddess of this tradition is elsewhere given a quite different address: an island of gems in an ocean of nectar, or the city of Śrīpura on the summit of Meru, described at length in the Lalitopākhyāna of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa. A further reading, widely current in the practice literature, identifies mahākailāsa with the sahasrāra, the thousand-petalled centre at the crown of the head where the ascent of the internal yoga terminates, so that the great Kailāsa is above the ordinary one in the same way that the crown is above the body. These readings are not rivals in the tradition's own view; the point of the qualifier is that whatever Kailāsa is, hers is the one it is a copy of.

Mṛṇāla is the fibrous inner thread of the lotus stalk, and it is one of the fixed similes of Sanskrit poetry, used for anything pale, cool and yielding. Court poets have their heroines wear bracelets and garlands of lotus fibre to cool the fever of separation, and the comparison of a woman's arm to a mṛṇāla is old enough by the classical period to be a convention rather than an observation. Dorlatā compounds dos, the arm, with latā, a creeper — the arm-as-vine, another stock figure, carrying the sense of something slender that curves and clings. What is notable is not the imagery, which any reader of kāvya has met a hundred times, but its position. The sahasranāma performs its physical description of the goddess near the beginning, working downwards from the hair, and by the five hundred and seventy-ninth name that business is long finished. The body returns here, unannounced, in the middle of a run of abstractions, and it returns as softness.

Mahanīyā looks like a third mahā- name in a verse that already has two, and it is not. It is a gerundive of the verbal root √mah, to make great, to magnify, to honour — an old root, at home in the Vedic hymns, from which mahat and mahiman also descend. The suffix -anīya forms the future passive participle: to be honoured, deserving honour. Sanskrit gerundives carry a flavour of obligation, and the difference between saying that someone is admirable and saying that someone is to be admired is the difference this name depends on.

Dayā is sympathy, the impulse to spare, the feeling that arises at the sight of suffering; mūrti is solid form, and it is the ordinary word for the image in a shrine. The compound is a karmadhāraya in which the two members are in apposition, so it does not say that she has compassion, or that compassion is one of her attributes, but that compassion is what she is shaped as — the form is the pity, and there is no residue of her left over that might be indifferent. The Devī Māhātmya makes the same identification in its long litany of the goddess who abides in all beings as consciousness, as hunger, as shame, as sleep, and, in one of the verses, as compassion.

Sāmrājya belongs to the old vocabulary of kingship. It is the abstract noun from samrāj, the paramount sovereign of the Vedic royal consecrations, and the ritual literature distinguishes it carefully from ordinary rule: a rājan governs a kingdom, a samrāj governs kings. The Śrīvidyā tradition takes that political vocabulary literally and builds a court around her, with a minister, a commander of the army and a walled capital, an apparatus most fully described in the Bhaṇḍāsura narrative. Śālin, the ending, comes from a root meaning to be eminent and means furnished with, abounding in; it is used of a person who wears a quality the way one wears a garment. The verse therefore ends by saying not that empire was given to her but that she is amply supplied with it, and the soft arms three names earlier are what keep that from being merely a claim about power.
commentary.practice:
The hardest thing in this verse is the second name, and it is hard in an interesting way. Mṛṇālamṛdudorlatā contains the vocalic ṛ twice in its first four syllables, both times after m. The ṛ is a vowel, held for one short beat, made with the tongue curled towards the roof of the mouth; it is not the sequence ri, and English speakers who substitute ri will find the word collapses. Then notice that the ṇ of mṛṇāla is retroflex, and it is retroflex precisely because of the ṛ that precedes it. The same rule turned the n of sākṣiṇī retroflex two verses ago. Saying mṛ-ṇā-la slowly, feeling the tongue stay curled from the vowel into the nasal, is the most efficient drill for this sound in the whole hymn.

Dorlatā hides a sandhi. The word for arm is dos, ending in s; before the voiced l of latā that s becomes r, giving dor-latā. The same transformation governs the join between the third and fourth names, where dayāmūrtiḥ before mahā- yields dayāmūrtir mahāsāmrājyaśālinī, run together without a pause. If you learned the previous verses you have met this rule already at bhaktanidhir niyantrī. Sanskrit does this consistently, and once you stop being surprised by it the printed line becomes easy to read aloud.

Mahāsāmrājyaśālinī has two clusters worth isolating. Mrā is labial m followed immediately by r, with no vowel between them; and jya is the voiced palatal j followed by the palatal glide y, both made at the same place in the mouth, so the tongue does not move between them. The three long ās in mahāsāmrājya must all be given their length or the eight-syllable quarter will not fill out.

In the archanā the five become mahākailāsanilayāyai, mṛṇālamṛdudorlatāyai, mahanīyāyai, dayāmūrtyai and mahāsāmrājyaśālinyai. Dayāmūrtyai repays a moment's attention if you noticed the oddity of bhaktanidhaye in the earlier verse. Mūrti and nidhi are both i-stems, but mūrti is feminine and takes the feminine dative in -yai, while nidhi is masculine and keeps -aye. The hymn does not regularise them, and the two forms sitting a few verses apart are as clear a lesson in Sanskrit gender as any grammar will give you.

What the verse asks of the reciter is chiefly a refusal to choose. There is a persistent impulse, when a hymn puts imperial sovereignty and lotus-fibre arms in the same four lines, to treat one of them as the real content and the other as ornament — to hear the softness as poetic decoration attached to a serious claim about power, or to hear the empire as a metaphor attached to a serious claim about tenderness. The verse gives no warrant for either. It states an address, a physical quality, an obligation, an identity and a status, in that order, at the same level of seriousness, and the middle term is the one that makes the sequence more than a list. A recitation that slows at mṛṇālamṛdudorlatā rather than hurrying through it to reach the grander names is reciting the verse the composer wrote.

crossReferences.source: Devī Māhātmya 5 (from the hymn of the gods at Suraṭha's request, the sequence beginning yā devī sarvabhūteṣu)
crossReferences.deva: या देवी सर्वभूतेषु दयारूपेण संस्थिता । नमस्तस्यै नमस्तस्यै नमस्तस्यै नमो नमः ॥
crossReferences.iast: yā devī sarvabhūteṣu dayārūpeṇa saṃsthitā | namas tasyai namas tasyai namas tasyai namo namaḥ ||
crossReferences.translation: To the goddess who abides in all beings in the form of compassion — to her salutation, to her salutation, to her again and again salutation.
crossReferences.relevance: The same grammatical move as dayāmūrtiḥ, made a few centuries earlier and at greater length. The litany does not say that the goddess is compassionate; it says she is present in every being as compassion, alongside the verses that make her present as hunger, as sleep, as error and as shame. Compassion is treated as a mode of her being rather than a disposition she has, which is exactly what a karmadhāraya compound asserts.

crossReferences.deva: भवानि त्वं दासे मयि वितर दृष्टिं सकरुणामिति स्तोतुं वाञ्छन् कथयति भवानि त्वमिति यः । तदैव त्वं तस्मै दिशसि निजसायुज्यपदवीं मुकुन्दब्रह्मेन्द्रस्फुटमकुटनीराजितपदाम् ॥
crossReferences.iast: bhavāni tvaṃ dāse mayi vitara dṛṣṭiṃ sakaruṇām iti stotuṃ vāñchan kathayati bhavāni tvam iti yaḥ | tadaiva tvaṃ tasmai diśasi nijasāyujyapadavīṃ mukundabrahmendrasphuṭamakuṭanīrājitapadām ||
crossReferences.translation: Bhavānī — wishing to praise you by saying, cast a compassionate glance on me, your servant, a man says only the two words bhavāni tvam; and at that very moment you grant him union with yourself, that state whose feet are lit by the flashing crowns of Viṣṇu, Brahmā and Indra.
crossReferences.relevance: The stanza turns on a grammatical joke, since bhavāni is both the vocative of her name and the first-person optative may I become, so that a devotee who begins to beg is heard as asking to be her and is given what he did not know he had said. It holds together the two ends of this verse. The compassionate glance is dayā, and the crowns of the three great gods lighting her feet are what sāmrājya means when it is not a metaphor.

references.title: India: A Sacred Geography
references.author: Diana L. Eck (Harmony Books, 2012)
references.note: The best single account of how Indian religious geography works — why a mountain or a river is repeated in many places at once, and why calling something the great Kailāsa is a normal move rather than a mystification. Read her chapters on mountains before deciding whether mahākailāsanilayā is a claim about Tibet.

references.title: An Anthology of Sanskrit Court Poetry: Vidyākara's Subhāṣitaratnakoṣa
references.author: tr. Daniel H. H. Ingalls (Harvard Oriental Series, 1965)
references.note: Read fifty pages of this and the second name of the verse stops looking exotic. Ingalls translates a thirteenth-century anthology of stanzas, with an introduction that explains the conventions — the arm as creeper, the lotus fibre as the standard of coolness and softness — and shows how a poet works inside them. Also one of the finest pieces of translated Sanskrit in English.

references.title: Encountering the Goddess: A Translation of the Devī-Māhātmya and a Study of Its Interpretation
references.author: Thomas B. Coburn (SUNY Press, 1991)
references.note: A close translation with a long study of how the text has actually been used. The chapter on the hymns is directly relevant here, since it examines the yā devī sarvabhūteṣu litany and asks what kind of claim it is making about the relation between the goddess and the qualities she is said to be present as.

references.title: Śiva: The Erotic Ascetic
references.author: Wendy Doniger O'Flaherty (Oxford University Press, 1973; originally Asceticism and Eroticism in the Mythology of Śiva)
references.note: Argumentative and sometimes overreaching, but unequalled at laying out the Purāṇic material about Śiva and Pārvatī on Kailāsa, including the Rāvaṇa episode. Useful here as background for what the name presupposes about who else lives on that mountain.

references.title: A Sanskrit-English Dictionary
references.author: Monier Monier-Williams (Oxford, 1899)
references.note: Look up √mah and follow the derivatives down: mahat, mahiman, mahanīya. It is the quickest way to see that the third name of this verse is not built on the prefix mahā- that opens the first and the last, but on the verb underlying all three.
